transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-10-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Anya (Redwood Product) — Carlos (CTO, Silverpine), Priya (ML Eng), Omar (Infra), Leah (Product)

---
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Um, quick intro, I'm Maya AE on the Redwood team, with Jordan who will do most of the demo, and Anya from product. How's everyone doing?
[00:09] Carlos Vega: Good, thanks. We got a busy Friday — appreciate you fitting us in.
[00:12] Priya Menon: Morning/afternoon. We want to focus on how we can get deterministic actions out of the model and safely call a motion planner tool.
[00:20] Jordan Liu: Perfect, that's exactly what we want to show — JSON mode for typed responses, the sandboxed tool invoker, and runtime fallbacks if latencies spike. We'll jump into the console and then a quick API snippet.

---
Context & qualification
[00:35] Maya Patel: Quick context questions — what's your current stack for inference and orchestration?
[00:39] Omar Haddad: We're mostly self-hosting on GCP, internal endpoints in Kubernetes, sometimes run into tail latency with large seq lengths cause our teleop sequences are bursty. We also have strict audit requirements — everything must be logged and keys rotate via Cloud KMS.
[00:54] Leah Kim: Product is driving for deterministic action sequences so the motion controller can act without human-in-the-loop. Latency targets are sub-200ms for short commands, and for longer planning it's OK to be a bit higher.
[01:08] Jordan Liu: Got it — so two distinct profiles: fast single-action inference for teleop, and longer planning traces. Redwood supports routing and variant models for exactly that — low-latency small-context variants, and richer planning variants for longer sequences. We'll show how JSON mode lets you validate and fall back if schema doesn't match.

---
Demo start: Console walkthrough (JSON mode)
[01:30] Jordan Liu: I'm switching to the Console — first thing, JSON mode toggle on the route. Here we create an "action schema" that defines the shape we expect: top-level object with action_type, target_coords [x,y,z], velocity, nonce, and optional metadata.
[01:50] Priya Menon: Are those enforced at runtime or just a soft suggestion?
[01:54] Jordan Liu: Runtime-enforced — the engine will validate output against the schema. If the output doesn't match, you can have a fallback policy: retry with adjusted temperature, map to a compatible model variant, or call a validator function. We call these Structured Output Policies.
[02:10] [02:13] (brief keyboard sounds)
[02:18] Carlos Vega: Can we shape the schema so it never returns free text that the controller would interpret? That's our main risk.
[02:24] Anya Romero: Yes — the sandboxed tool invoker only accepts machine-readable JSON fits the schema; free text is flagged and can trigger a fail-safe. We also let you define enums for action_type to restrict to allowed ops (MOVE, ROTATE, GRIP).

---
Tool / function calling demo (sandbox)
[02:42] Jordan Liu: Now I'll demo a function call integration — we wire a motion-planner service as a 'tool'. The model returns a 'tool_call' object with the tool name and params, Redwood's runtime will serialize that and invoke the approved tool only inside a sandbox.
[02:59] Priya Menon: Sandbox how? Network egress restrictions?
[03:03] Jordan Liu: Two layers — logical sandbox in the runtime prevents arbitrary exec and enforces a whitelist of tool APIs, plus in Private mode you can run the tool inside your VPC/on-prem and Redwood will only signal the invocation. So no direct external egress from your environment unless you enable it.
[03:20] Omar Haddad: That helps. Our security team also requires HSM-backed key management and per-request audit logs.
[03:27] Maya Patel: We integrate with KMS/HSM and provide token-level traces you can forward into your SIEM. We'll drop our security pack after this call.

---
Schema enforcement + fallback policies
[03:40] Jordan Liu: Showing an example — model tries to return an array for target_coords but the schema expects an object with x,y,z. Console highlights the validation failure, and the policy shows three options: auto-retry with deterministic decoding parameters, fallback to an L1 low-latency variant with different tokenization, or call a small validator lambda to map legacy formats.
[04:05] Leah Kim: Would retry add latency and cause action duplication risk?
[04:08] Jordan Liu: Good question — we do idempotency keys and request dedup so retries are safe. For strict teleop paths we recommend "no-retry" and immediate fallback to a conservative safe action (e.g., STOP) plus alerting.

---
API snippet + telemetry
[04:30] Jordan Liu: Quick API view — here's a sample call: model: aurora-mini-llm-ll, mode: json, schema_id: motion-v1, fallback_policy: to_stop_on_mismatch. The response contains 'structured_data' and a 'tool_call' field. You can capture token-level cost and latency per-call in the Console, filter by schema, and set alerts if error-rate for schema validation exceeds X%.
[04:58] Carlos Vega: You mentioned aurora-mini-llm-ll — is that a Redwood model or a proxied open model?
[05:03] Jordan Liu: It's Redwood-verified variant — in Hosted we provide curated models; in Dedicated you can bring-your-own or use our variant that is quantized for low-latency. If you need on-prem we support Private with the same API semantics.

---
Failure modes and graceful degradation
[05:25] Jordan Liu: Let's talk about graceful degradation: if the primary model or region goes down or latency spikes above the policy, Smart Routing can reroute to a cheaper slightly higher-latency region, or to a deterministic small model pinned for safety. In the Console you can simulate capacity constraints and define the behavior per route.
[05:46] Priya Menon: For teleop we can't afford region hops. Is there a local edge option?
[05:50] Jordan Liu: Yep — Dedicated pools deployed into your preferred region and Private deployments in your VPC give you that locality. Redwood's autoscaling can ensure reserved capacity for teleop routes.

---
Optimize recommendations (cost vs latency)
[06:10] Anya Romero: From Optimize, we'd suggest quantizing planning models to int8 and using prefix KV cache for repeated map queries. For teleop, configuring micro-batching to 1 and enabling early-exit tokens reduces tail latency. The Console's Optimize tab gives estimates on cost savings per-config change.
[06:33] Omar Haddad: Micro-batching of 1—does that increase per-token cost?
[06:37] Anya Romero: Slightly, but the tradeoff is improved P95 latency. Optimize shows the delta; often for teleop the latency wins outweigh cost.

---
Security / compliance specifics
[06:52] Maya Patel: Quick checkpoint on compliance — Redwood is SOC 2 compliant and supports enterprise SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integration, and detailed request audit logs. For Private we can do additional controls for air-gapped environments.
[07:07] Carlos Vega: Our procurement will want a SOC 2 attestation and network diagram.
[07:11] Maya Patel: We'll include that in the security pack.

---
Live sandbox run (simulated teleop)
[07:20] Jordan Liu: I'll run a simulation — prompt: "move to target at [1.2, -0.4, 0.33] with velocity 0.5". Model returns structured action: action_type: MOVE, target_coords: {x:1.2, y:-0.4, z:0.33}, velocity:0.5, nonce: "abc123". Console shows the tool_call to /motion-planner, payload serialized.
[07:50] Priya Menon: Nice. What if the model hallucinated a free-text explanation?
[07:55] Jordan Liu: In JSON mode the runtime strips free text and flags a schema violation. The fallback policy we bound to 'STOP' and emit an alert.
[08:03] [08:06] (murmur)

---
Edge case: partial matches and hybrid outputs
[08:15] Jordan Liu: Sometimes outputs are hybrid — e.g., valid JSON plus trailing commentary. You can set the parser to strict (reject) or permissive (extract first valid object). For safety-critical paths we always recommend strict parsing.
[08:33] Carlos Vega: We'll need strict.

---
Questions from customer
[08:45] Priya Menon: Could we run a small PoC where Redwood handles planning but we keep teleop on-prem? Basically split the pipeline.
[08:54] Maya Patel: Absolutely — that's a common hybrid approach. We can set up a Dedicated route for teleop and Hosted or Private for planning, with routing policy that pins teleop to Dedicated.
[09:05] Omar Haddad: How do we manage keys across hosted and private? We don't want plaintext keys anywhere.
[09:10] Jordan Liu: For Private you'd manage keys in your KMS; Redwood only stores references and supports envelope encryption and HSM-backed key wrap. For Hosted we offer customer-managed keys in some tiers.

---
Performance benchmarking and pilot scope
[09:28] Jordan Liu: For the pilot we usually do 2 weeks: week 1 schema + integration (console + tool wiring), week 2 stress + latency benchmarks and safety validation. We'll run a small benchmark suite that mimics your bursty teleop patterns and report P50/P95/P99, plus schema validation rates.
[09:47] Leah Kim: We'll need the benchmark script so we can run internally too.
[09:51] Jordan Liu: We'll share that.

---
Objections and trade-offs
[10:00] Carlos Vega: Our infra team is wary of vendor lock-in. If we build workflows around Redwood features like prefix KV or routing policies, is it easy to extract?
[10:11] Maya Patel: Good point — we export configs as YAML and provide runbooks for migrating logic. Also, for Private you can have the same runtime on-prem with the same APIs, so migration is minimized.
[10:24] Priya Menon: Another concern — how deterministic is the JSON output across model updates?
[10:29] Jordan Liu: We version model variants and pin by commit. Console lets you pin a route to a model version; we also recommend evaluation suites to detect regressions before rolling out. Optimize can notify you if schema pass rates drop after a rollout.

---
Recap and explicit next steps
[10:50] Maya Patel: Quick recap — we'll send: pilot pricing + SOW, security pack, console recording, schema examples, and the benchmark runner. Jordan to share the console recording and schema lib; I'll send pricing. Carlos will gather the 3 canonical workflows and success metrics. We aim to kick off the pilot the week of Oct 23rd.
[11:14] Carlos Vega: Sounds good. Can we get a short technical sync during integration week? 30–40 mins?
[11:19] Jordan Liu: Yes, we'll schedule an SE-led kickoff to wire the tool and run the first schema test.

---
Loose transcript (remaining minutes; highlights)
[11:30] Priya Menon: Slight aside — do you support custom tokenizers for our quantized models?
[11:35] Jordan Liu: We support custom tokenization paths in Dedicated and Private, yes.
[11:38] Omar Haddad: Any restrictions on model size for Private?
[11:41] Anya Romero: We can deploy up to large-family models but matrix sizing requires planning; we'll include config notes in SOW.
[11:49] Carlos Vega: Competitors: we've looked at Anthropic and OpenAI pipelines; main differences are per-call telemetry and rollback tooling which you guys highlight.
[11:57] Maya Patel: Right — we focus on runtime observability and predictable economics.

---
Closing
[12:05] Maya Patel: Thank you everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts. Expect the security pack and pricing in the next couple days.
[12:11] Leah Kim: Thanks, talk soon.
[12:13] Carlos Vega: Appreciate it.
[12:15] (call ends)

Note: timestamps above reflect transcript offsets; full call contained additional short Q&A and follow-up clarifications. Transcription may contain minor mis-hearings (model names, some param names).
